'''Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Green | first1 = M. L. H. | authorlink1 = Malcolm Green (chemist)| last2 = Griffith | first2 = W. P. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1999.0103 | title = Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson. 14 July 1921 -- 26 September 1996: Elected 18 March 1965 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 46 | pages = 593–606 | year = 2000 | doi-access = free }}</ref> (14 July 1921 – 26 September 1996) was a [[Nobel laureate]] English [[chemist]] who pioneered [[inorganic chemistry]] and homogeneous [[transition metal]] [[catalysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/ic961299i | title = Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson 1921−1996 IN MEMORIAM | journal = Inorganic Chemistry | volume = 35 | issue = 26 | pages = 7463–7464 | year = 1996 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.patentgenius.com/inventor/WilkinsonGeoffrey.html |title=Geoffrey Wilkinson Patents |access-date=31 October 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107022739/http://www.patentgenius.com/inventor/WilkinsonGeoffrey.html |archive-date=7 November 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Wilkinson was born at Springside, [[Todmorden]], in the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]]. His father, Henry Wilkinson, was a master [[house painter and decorator]]; his mother, Ruth, worked in a local [[cotton mill]]. One of his uncles, an organist and [[Conducting|choirmaster]], had married into a family that owned a small chemical company making [[Magnesium sulfate|Epsom]] and [[Sodium sulfate|Glauber]]'s salts for the [[pharmaceutical industry]]; this is where he first developed an interest in chemistry.

He was educated at the local council primary school and, after winning a County Scholarship in 1932, went to [[Todmorden Grammar School]]. His [[physics]] teacher there, Luke Sutcliffe, had also taught Sir [[John Cockcroft]], who received a Nobel Prize for "splitting the atom". In 1939 he obtained a Royal Scholarship for study at [[Imperial College London]], from where he graduated in 1941, with his PhD awarded in 1946 entitled "Some physico-chemical observations of hydrolysis in the homogeneous vapour phase".<ref>{{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.587112}}</ref><ref name="NobelFoundationBio" /><ref>{{cite web |title=GENEALOGY DATABASE ENTRY – Wikinson, Geoffrey |url=https://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/Web_Genealogy/Info/wilkinsong.pdf |website=scs.illinois.edu |last1=Mainz |first1=Vera V. |last2=Girolami |first2=Gregory S. |date=1988}}</ref>

==Career and research==
In 1942 Professor [[Friedrich Paneth]] was recruiting young chemists for the [[Nuclear power|nuclear energy]] project. Wilkinson joined and was sent out to Canada, where he stayed in [[Montreal]] and later [[Chalk River Laboratories]] until he could leave in 1946. For the next four years he worked with Professor [[Glenn T. Seaborg]] at [[University of California, Berkeley]], mostly on nuclear taxonomy.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/643851/Sir-Geoffrey-Wilkinson |title = Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson &#124; British chemist| date=10 July 2023 }}</ref> He then became a research associate at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and began to return to his first interest as a student – [[Complex (chemistry)|transition metal complex]]es of [[ligand]]s such as [[carbon monoxide]] and [[olefin]]s.

He was at [[Harvard University]] from September 1951 until he returned to England in December 1955, with a sabbatical break of nine months in [[Copenhagen]]. At Harvard, he still did some nuclear work on excitation functions for [[proton]]s in [[cobalt]], but had already begun to work on olefin complexes.

In June 1955 he was appointed to the chair of Inorganic Chemistry at [[Imperial College London]], and from then on worked almost entirely on the complexes of transition metals.

Wilkinson is well known for his popularisation of the use of [[Wilkinson's catalyst]] RhCl(PPh<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> in catalytic hydrogenation, and for the discovery of the structure of [[ferrocene]]. Wilkinson's catalyst is used industrially in the [[hydrogenation]] of [[alkenes]] to [[alkanes]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=F.H. |last=Jardine |title=The Contributions of Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson, F.R.S., (1921–1996) to Rhodium Chemistry |journal=Rhodium Express |volume=16 |pages=4–10 |year=1996 |url=http://sites.google.com/site/rhodiumexpress/ |issn=0869-7876 |access-date=11 September 2010 |archive-date=23 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220623191029/https://sites.google.com/site/rhodiumexpress/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Osborn|first1= J. A.|last2= Jardine|first2= F. H.|last3= Young|first3= J. F.|last4= Wilkinson|first4= G.| title=The Preparation and Properties of Tris(triphenylphosphine)halogenorhodium(I) and Some Reactions Thereof Including Catalytic Homogeneous Hydrogenation of Olefins and Acetylenes and Their Derivatives| journal= [[Journal of the Chemical Society A]] | year = 1966 | pages = 1711–1732 | doi = 10.1039/J19660001711}}</ref>

Osborn]], [[Alan Davison]]<ref name=davisonphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|website=ethos.bl.uk|publisher=Imperial College London|title=Studies on the chemistry of transition metal carbonyls|first= Alan|last=Davison|year=1962|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.602048|hdl=10044/1/13205}}</ref><ref name=davison>{{cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Malcolm L. H.|authorlink1=Malcolm Green (chemist)|last2=Cummins|first2=Christopher C.|last3=Kronauge|first3=James F.|title=Alan Davison. 24 March 1936 – 14 November 2015|journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]|volume=63|pages=197–213|year=2017|issn=0080-4606|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2017.0004|doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[Malcolm Green (chemist)|Malcolm Green]].<ref name=greenphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|website=london.ac.uk|publisher=Imperial College London|title=A study of some transitional metal hydrides and olefin complexes|first= Malcolm Leslie Hodder Green|last=Green|year=1958|url=http://catalogue.libraries.london.ac.uk/record=b2995428}}</ref> Cotton and Wilkinson collaborated on the book ''"Advanced Inorganic Chemistry"'', often referred to simply as "Cotton and Wilkinson", one of the standard inorganic chemistry textbooks.<ref>{{Cite book

==Awards and honours==
Throughout his career, Wilkinson received many prestigious awards, including the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] in 1973<ref name="NobelFoundationBio">{{cite web | title=Geoffrey Wilkinson – Autobiography | website=nobelprize.org | date=11 October 2012 | url=http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1973/wilkinson-autobio.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011193653/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1973/wilkinson-autobio.html | archive-date=11 October 2012 | url-status=dead | access-date=20 July 2021}}</ref> for his work on "[[organometallic compound]]s" (with [[Ernst Otto Fischer]]). Prior to winning the Nobel Prize, he had been elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1965|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS)]] in 1965. In 1968, he won the [[Lavoisier Medal]], awarded by the [[Société chimique de France|Chemical Society of France]]. In 1981, he received the [[Royal Medal]] from the [[Royal Society]] as well as the [[Ludwig Mond Award]] from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="frs" /> 

Wilkinson was made a [[Knight Bachelor]] by [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] in the [[1976 Birthday Honours]].<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=46919|date= 12 June 1976|supp=1|page=8016}}</ref> Despite his knighthood, he did not consider himself part of the "establishment"<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1996-01-01 |title=Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson 1921−1996 IN MEMORIAM |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ic961299i |journal=Inorganic Chemistry |volume=35 |issue=26 |pages=7463–7464 |doi=10.1021/ic961299i |issn=0020-1669 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and remained vocally critical of successive British prime ministers, education ministers and university vice-chancellors for insufficient support and funding for the sciences.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last= |author-link= |date=2020-03-05 |title=College chemistry Nobel Laureates honoured with presentation of plaques |url=https://www.rsc.org/news-events/articles/2007/05-may/nobel-laureates/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250417102416/https://www.rsc.org/news-events/articles/2007/05-may/nobel-laureates/ |archive-date=2025-04-17 |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |language=en}}</ref>

Wilkinson also received honorary doctorates and fellowships from several universities, including:
* [[Columbia University]] - [[Doctor of Science|DSc]], 1978<ref>{{Cite news |last=Johnston |first=Laurie |date=1978-05-18 |title=Commencement 1978 at Columbia Hears an Echo of 1968 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/05/18/archives/commencement-1978-at-columbia-hears-an-echo-of-1968-students-at.html |access-date=2026-04-11 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>
* [[University of Bath]] - DSc, 1980<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorary graduates, 1980 to 1989 |url=https://www.bath.ac.uk/corporate-information/honorary-graduates-1980-to-1989/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=[[University of Bath]]}}</ref>
* [[University of Essex]] - Honorary Doctorate, 1989<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorary graduates |url=https://www.essex.ac.uk/alumni/honorary/honorary-graduates |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250815060219/https://www.essex.ac.uk/alumni/honorary/honorary-graduates |archive-date=2025-08-15 |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=[[University of Essex]] |language=en}}</ref>
* Imperial College London - Honorary fellowship, 1993<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorary graduates, fellows and Imperial College medals |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/about/introducing-imperial/our-people/honorary-graduates-and-fellows/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=[[Imperial College London]]}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Wilkinson was married to Lise Schou, a Danish plant physiologist whom he had met at UC Berkeley. They had two daughters, Anne and Pernille.<ref name="frs"/>

==Legacy and commemoration==
Since 1999, the Royal Society of Chemistry has been awarding the annual Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Prize (formerly the Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Lectureship), aimed at celebrating contributions to any area of inorganic chemistry made by a mid-career scientist. The first winner of this prize was Professor [[Malcolm Green (chemist)|Malcolm Green]], one of Wilkinson's former students.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dalton mid-career prize: Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Prize |url=https://www.rsc.org/standards-and-recognition/prizes/research-and-innovation-prizes/dalton-mid-career-prize-sir-geoffrey-wilkinson-prize |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |language=en}}</ref> Since 2022, Imperial College London has been hosting the annual Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Lecture.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Lecture |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/whats-on/about-imperial-events/our-events/annual-lectures/the-sir-geoffrey-wilkinson-lecture-/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=Imperial College London |language=en-GB}}</ref> Both the Royal Society of Chemistry prize and the annual lecture at Imperial are funded by the Geoffery Wilkinson Charitable Foundation, run by Professor Anne Hardy, one of Wilkinson's daughters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About the foundation |url=https://wilkinsonfoundation.org.uk/home/about/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=Wilkinson Foundation |language=}}</ref> Since 2016, the foundation has also been funding an annual PhD studentship at Imperial in the field of inorganic chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Overton |first=Isabel |date=2022-12-07 |title=Chemistry receives £1m gift in honour of alumnus Professor Geoffrey Wilkinson |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/242192/chemistry-receives-1m-gift-honour-alumnus/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=[[Imperial College London]] |language=en-GB}}</ref>

A blue plaque was installed at 4 Wellington Road, [[Todmorden]] in 1990, marking Wilkinson's childhood home.<ref name="frs" /> In 2007, the Royal Society of Chemistry erected a plaque at [[Department of Chemistry, Imperial College London|Imperial College London's Chemistry Building]] in honour of Wilkinson as part of its [[List of blue plaques erected by the Royal Society of Chemistry#Chemical Landmark Scheme|Chemical Landmark Scheme]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson |url=https://www.londonremembers.com/memorials/sir-geoffrey-wilkinson/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=London Remembers |language=en}}</ref> Imperial College's [[Imperial College Halls of Residence#Eastside|Wilkinson Hall]], opened in 2009, is named in the chemist's honour.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wilkinson |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/students/student-support-zone/support/in-your-halls/wilkinson/ |access-date=2026-04-10 |website=Imperial College London |language=en-GB}}</ref>
